newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to open wider bond market to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to open wider bond market to foreigners.

text.p: South Korea plans to allow domestic small and medium-sized firms to issue non-guaranteed corporate bonds exclusively for foreign investors, effective January 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said on Sunday.
The plan is in line with Seoul's years-long drive to gradually open up its capital markets to foreigners, the ministry said in a statement.

At the same time, the ceiling of aggregate foreign investment in convertible bonds issued by domestic listed small and medium-sized firms will be raised to 50 percent of the total amount issued from 30 percent at present, it said.
It also said the individual ceiling would be doubled to 10 percent of a company's convertible bonds issued from the current five percent.
Eligible to apply to issue corporate bonds exclusively for foreign investors will be those listed on the Korea Stock Exchange or on the over-the-counter market.
A rating of BB or higher from one of three domestic credit rating services will also be a prerequisite for a firm to apply to South Korea's Securities and Exchange Commission, it said.
Approval from the commission will also be required on the amount of bonds to be issued and commercial terms on them.
The ministry said it expected the plan to help domestic small and medium-sized firms raise funds and ultimately to contribute to bringing down domestic interest rates.
Interest rates in South Korea are among the highest in Asia. Bank lending rates currently stand at over 12 percent in South Korea.

The ministry also reaffirmed its earlier plan to allow foreign investment in long-term non-guaranteed straight bonds issued by small and medium-sized firms in 1997, non-guaranteed convertible bonds issued by large firms in 1998 and non-guaranteed straight bonds issued by large firms in 1999.
